Earth is the
third
planet from the Sun, located between Venus and Mars.

The centrifugal force is maximum at the equator.

Mercury and Venus have no natural satellites.
A Blue Moon is defined as two full moons occurring in one calendar month.
Halley’s Comet has a period of about 76 years, whereas Hale-Bopp has a long period of about 2,534 years.
Apollo 11
made the first human landing on the Moon in 1969, at the Sea of Tranquility.
The main components of the Solar System are the Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, satellites, asteroids, comets, meteoroids and cosmic dust.
Gravity is the force responsible for keeping bodies in orbit.
The outer planets in order are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Jupiter
has the highest gravitational acceleration.

The revolution periods are Mercury—88 days, Venus—224.7 days, Earth—365.25 days and Mars—687 days.

Neptune has the slowest orbital velocity.
Venus is known as the Earth-twin.
Earth lies between Venus and Mars, and its shape is described as a geoid or oblate spheroid.
Earth’s equatorial diameter is 12,756 km, its polar diameter is 12,714 km, its equatorial circumference is 40,090 km, and its axial tilt is 23.5°.
Earth revolves around the Sun in 365.25 days, producing a year and seasons, and its mean orbital velocity is 29.8 km/s.
The mean Earth–Sun distance is 149.6 million km, and this distance is defined as one astronomical unit.
Earth’s habitable zone is called the Goldilocks Zone.
Earth is the only known life-supporting planet, and rotation means the spinning of Earth on its axis.
The daily cycle is associated with rotation.
Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere on 21 March.
21 June is the Northern Hemisphere summer solstice and 22 December is the Northern Hemisphere winter solstice.
Day and night are approximately equal during the equinoxes.
The Sun is a star at the centre of the Solar System.
The Sun’s core temperature is 15 million°C and its interior is in a plasma state.
The Sun accounts for 99.8% of the Solar System’s mass and its diameter is 109 times Earth’s diameter.
The corona is visible during a solar eclipse, while a sunspot is a dark patch on the photosphere.
Perihelion is reached in early January, whereas aphelion is reached in early July.
One astronomical unit equals approximately 149.6 × 10⁹ m.
Earth’s greater width at the equator and flattening at the poles describe its oblate spheroid or geoid shape.
The crust contains 46.6% oxygen.
The mantle lies below the crust; the outer core contains liquid iron and nickel; the inner core contains solid iron; and the core has a depth of 2,900 km.
Aristotle
was the first stated source for Earth’s spherical shape.
Aryabhatta linked Earth's rotation with the Sun's daily motion; Thumba is a tested geomagnetic-equator location; and Earth Day is observed on 22 April, first observed in 1970.
Alpha Centauri is the next closest star mentioned after the Sun.

The Moon's diameter is 3,475 km; its average distance is 384,400 km; its minimum and maximum distances are 363,300 km and 405,500 km; and its orbital and rotation period is 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes.
The Moon shows the same face toward Earth.
Perigee is the Moon's closest position to Earth, apogee is its farthest position, and a supermoon is a full Moon near perigee.
The Moon's atmosphere is essentially absent, and its gravity is one-sixth of Earth's gravity.
A lunar eclipse is visible over a larger part of the night side, the corona is specially visible during a total solar eclipse, and the Moon may appear reddish during a lunar eclipse.
A half moon occurs when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 90°.
At perigee, the Moon produces stronger gravity and higher tides.
Asteroids are composed of rock and metal and generally have less eccentric orbits.
Comets are associated with the outer system, asteroids generally lack tails, and comets develop tails near the Sun, with the tail directed away from the Sun.
Radiation pressure and solar wind cause the comet’s tail to point away from the Sun.
The Rosetta mission targeted
67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko
A meteor is popularly called a
shooting star
Galileo studied the Galilean moons.
Johann Galle is associated with
Neptune
Mercury is the smallest, Venus is the hottest, Neptune is the coldest and Earth is the densest planet.
Sunlight takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach Earth.
Halley’s Comet last appeared in 1986.
An aurora is produced when solar particles interact with the atmosphere.

Earth’s orbital speed is greater at perihelion.
The Northern Hemisphere winter solstice occurs approximately on 21 or 22 December.
Rotation produces time zones.
Earth’s two primary motions are rotation and revolution.
Earth’s axis is the imaginary line joining the North and South Poles.
Day and night result from Earth’s rotation, with the Sun-facing side illuminated and the opposite side dark.
Earth rotates through 1° every 4 minutes.
Moving objects are deflected to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Coriolis effect is applicable to both winds and ocean currents.
The centrifugal effect is caused by Earth’s rotation, is maximum at the Equator, minimum or zero at the Poles, and contributes to polar flattening.
Earth’s axis is an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, and it makes an angle of 66.5° with the orbital plane.
Earth follows an elliptical orbit around the Sun.

The Summer Solstice is associated with the Tropic of Cancer and opposite day-length conditions in the two hemispheres; the Winter Solstice is associated with the Tropic of Capricorn and the reverse pattern.

Equinoxes occur twice a year with approximately equal day and night; the March Equinox marks spring in the Northern Hemisphere and autumn in the Southern Hemisphere, while the September Equinox marks autumn in the Northern Hemisphere.
The Sun is overhead at the Equator on 23 September.
The North Pole has six months of continuous daylight.
Continuous daylight occurs beyond the Arctic Circle during Northern Hemisphere summer and beyond the Antarctic Circle during Southern Hemisphere summer.
Summer receives greater solar energy and has greater heating, whereas winter receives lower solar energy and has lower heating.
Aphelion means that Earth is farthest from the Sun.
Earth’s maximum speed at perihelion is explained by Kepler’s Second Law.
A normal year has 365 days, the yearly extra fraction is one-quarter of a day, and its accumulation produces a 366-day leap year with 29 February as the extra day.
The Equator is at 0° latitude.
The centrifugal effect causes equatorial bulging and polar flattening.
Longitude difference produces local-time difference.
The length of day has changed by a very small measurable amount.
Ice-sheet melting redistributes mass and water toward lower latitudes.
Rotation has an indirect seasonal role.
Weight increases toward the Poles.
Earth’s rotation produces time differences: local time advances when moving east, and time advances eastward.
The seasonal cycle results from Earth’s revolution, its axial tilt and the approximate parallelism of its axis.
The direct rays of the Sun fall on the Equator during an equinox.

Seasons occur due to Earth’s revolution around the Sun combined with its axial tilt of 23½°.
Earth revolves around the Sun in approximately
365.25 days
On 21 June, the Sun is vertically overhead at the
Tropic of Cancer
, at 23½°N latitude.
At the Equator,
day and night are approximately 12 hours each throughout the year
The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word Mausim, meaning
season
Rotation on its axis causes day and night.
Earth’s revolution must operate together with its axial tilt to produce seasonal changes.
Summer solar rays are more direct.
Differential heating and cooling of land and sea is identified as the main mechanism behind the seasonal reversal of monsoon winds.
The June solstice corresponds to the Tropic of Cancer and the December solstice to the Tropic of Capricorn.
The vertical Sun is at the Equator on 21 March.
Rabi is sown in October–November, Kharif in June–July, and Zaid is grown between Rabi and Kharif.
Around 21 June, the Northern Hemisphere has its longest day, while the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day; the Arctic region can experience continuous daylight.
Land and sea breezes are daily or diurnal phenomena.
The Equator has nearly equal day and night throughout the year and is characterized more by wet and dry seasons than by distinct winter and summer.
The vertical Sun is at the Tropic of Capricorn on 21 or 22 December.
The axis is inclined at 66½° to the orbital plane, while Earth is tilted by 23½° as it revolves around the Sun.
The main consequence of Earth’s revolution and axial tilt is a changing angle of insolation during the year.
During revolution, the approximately parallel axial tilt causes the two hemispheres to alternately tilt toward and away from the Sun.
Summer solar energy has greater concentration.
Seasonal variation involves changing day length, longer illumination for one hemisphere at a time, changing heating, and the production of seasons by that changing heating.
Continuous daylight at the Arctic Circle and beyond can last six months.
Solstices and equinoxes each occur twice per year; the solstitial overhead position is at one of the tropics, while the equinoctial overhead position is at the Equator.
On 21 March, the Sun is overhead at the Equator and starts moving northward.
The Northern Hemisphere’s longest day usually occurs on 20 or 21 June.
Around June, the North Pole experiences continuous daylight.
Polar day lasts approximately six months.

The midnight sun occurs in the polar regions, is strongest around the relevant summer solstice, can produce 24-hour daylight, and is experienced in places such as Norway as well as other polar regions.
The Sun remains above the horizon during polar day.
The angular distance from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn is 47°.
At the December solstice, the noon altitude at the Tropic of Cancer is
Slanting solar rays spread energy over a larger area, resulting in lower heating.
The winter hemisphere receives more oblique rays and has shorter days.
A higher Sun produces a smaller shadow, while a lower Sun produces a longer shadow.
Christmas is summer in Australia.
Perihelion is the position of minimum Earth–Sun distance, while aphelion is the position of maximum distance.
Perihelion occurs approximately on 4 January and orbital speed is faster there.
Distance from the Sun does not primarily cause seasons.
A
monsoon
is defined as a seasonal reversal of wind pattern.
The southwest monsoon occurs from June to September, while the retreating monsoon occurs from October to November.
The Indian traditional rainy season lasts from July to August.
Kharif crops are harvested in October and November, and Zaid crops belong to a short summer season.
Mountain and valley breezes are periodic, summer heating produces low pressure, and winter cooling produces high pressure.
Seasonal rainfall associated with a monsoonal climate produces alternating wet and dry seasons.

Seasonal wind reversal produces monsoons; seasonal crop cycles include Rabi, Kharif and Zaid; seasonal vegetation includes tropical deciduous forests; and seasonal temperature is related to insolation and day length.
An equinox is a transition point between seasons.

The
mantle
lies below the crust and is predominantly solid, with plastic behaviour over geological time.
Oxygen constitutes 46.60% of Earth’s crust by weight.
S-waves cannot travel through liquids, and their disappearance provides evidence that the outer core is liquid.
Mechanical layering is represented by the lithosphere, asthenosphere, deeper mantle, outer core and inner core.
Continental crust is generally older, not younger, than oceanic crust.
The Mohorovicic or Moho discontinuity separates the crust and mantle.
Magma is molten rock below the surface; after reaching the surface, it is called
lava
Mantle movement drives plate movement.
S-waves are also called transverse or shear waves.
Oceanic crust has higher, not lower, density than continental crust.

Movement and convection of conducting material in the liquid outer core produce the geodynamo.
The core begins at approximately
depth.
New crust is added by seafloor spreading, while old crust is destroyed by subduction.
Earth’s crust is the outermost layer.
The broad composition of the crust includes oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron, and other elements.
Calcium constitutes 3.63% and ranks fifth; sodium 2.83% and sixth; potassium 2.59% and seventh; and magnesium 2.09% and eighth by weight.
The main constituent of the core is iron.
Continental crust forms the continents, whereas oceanic crust forms the ocean floors.
The mantle has a major role in plate tectonics.
The lithosphere is the rigid upper zone and consists of the crust and uppermost mantle.
The lithosphere is relatively strong, is broken into plates, and is described as an earthquake-generating shell.
P-waves are primary waves and are also called compressional or longitudinal waves.
A volcano is an outlet for magma, lava and gases.
Surface waves are the slowest seismic waves.
P-wave particles vibrate parallel to propagation and have a longitudinal push–pull nature.
P-waves are strongly refracted at the mantle–core boundary.
The P-wave shadow zone is also given as approximately 105°–140°.
Earthquakes generate seismic waves.
A sudden velocity increase is the seismic clue for the Moho discontinuity.
The 410-kilometre and 660-kilometre discontinuities mark mineralogical zones in the mantle, and phase changes are associated with these zones.
Earth’s average density is approximately 5.5 g/cm³, its density increases inward, and heavier materials are concentrated in the core; Earth is the densest planet.
Internal heat produces endogenic processes.
Endogenic processes drive mantle dynamics.
Plate movement produces folding, faulting, earthquakes, volcanism, and mountain building.
The asthenosphere allows lithospheric plates to move.
Igneous rocks form by cooling or solidification, sedimentary rocks by surface deposition, metamorphic rocks by heat or pressure, granite is intrusive and basalt is extrusive.
Magma produces volcanism; the mantle lies below the crust; a volcano releases lava, ash and gases; and water vapour is the most abundant volcanic gas.
Lava is dominated by
silica
The outer core is mainly composed of
iron and nickel
The asthenosphere is mechanically weaker and is described as weak or ductile, allowing lithospheric plate movement.
The geodynamo generates Earth’s magnetic field.

The
Tibetan Plateau
is identified as the highest plateau, with an average elevation of 4,500 m.
The Himalayas are young fold mountains.
Compression produces folding, forming the high, rugged and steep character associated with young fold mountains.
The Deccan Plateau has a predominantly basaltic volcanic origin, while the Chotanagpur Plateau is mineral-rich and drained by the Damodar.
A blind valley is a karst or limestone feature, not a tectonic feature.
The Aravallis are old fold mountains.
The Narmada Valley is a rift-valley example.
Deposition forms deltas at river mouths.
Delta, meander and alluvial fan are associated with running water.
A cirque is a bowl-shaped hollow.
Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes, while seifs are long, narrow longitudinal dunes.
A
stalagmite
rises from the cave floor, whereas a stalactite hangs from the cave roof.
The Northern Plains are vast alluvial depositional plains.
Yardang is a streamlined ridge, mushroom rock has a narrow base and wider top, playa is a dry lake bed, and loess is a fine silt deposit.
Divergence and faulting cause the central block to subside, producing the elongated depression called a rift valley.
A
tombolo
is a depositional bar connecting an island to the mainland.
Fuji is a volcanic mountain, so the count is three.

Malwa lies between the Aravalli and Vindhya, Chotanagpur is mineral-rich and drained by the Damodar, Dandakaranya is a central-eastern highland, and Bhander is the southern part of the Vindhyan scarpland.
Caves or caverns are underground dissolution features.
Intermontane plateaus are enclosed or surrounded by mountains.
A sea cliff forms through wave erosion, a sea cave through erosion of weak zones, a sea arch when a cave enlarges through a headland, and a sea stack after an arch collapses.
The
Andes
in South America are identified as the longest major mountain range.
The formation of mountains involves
folding, erosion, faulting and volcanism
The Alps are major mountains.
The Pamir Plateau is a major plateau.
Plains result from deposition, erosion and marine processes.
Valleys are formed by rivers, glaciers, tectonic processes and karst processes.
V-shaped valleys are river landforms.
Canyons are formed by erosion, transportation, and deposition processes.
Waterfall
s are identified as river landforms in the classification of major landforms.
Glacial erosion and deposition produce landforms such as arêtes, horns, U-shaped valleys, hanging valleys and moraines.
Yardangs are desert landforms.
Sand dunes are accumulations of sand.
Loess
is classified as a desert landform associated with wind deposition.
Karst or groundwater forms sinkholes.
Coastal landforms are formed by waves, currents, and tides.
Cliffs, caves, arches and stacks are erosional coastal landforms, while beaches are depositional coastal landforms.
Spits and lagoons are classified as coastal landforms.
Old fold mountains are highly eroded.
The Appalachians, Urals and Pennines are old fold mountains, while the Salt Range is a block mountain.
Volcanic mountains form through accumulation of lava and volcanic material and characteristically have conical peaks.
Residual mountains form when erosion removes weaker material and leaves resistant rocks behind.
Residual mountains are remnants of older elevated surfaces; the Appalachians and Pennines are residual mountains.
Dome mountains have dome-shaped uplift, and the Black Hills and Bighorns are examples of dome mountains.
The Sierra Nevada are block mountains.
The Rhine Valley and the Vosges form a block mountain–rift valley system.
Block mountains consist of uplifted blocks.
Volcanic mountains typically have
cones
Craters are associated with volcanic mountains.
The Tibetan Plateau is intermontane, the Piedmont Plateau of the USA is piedmont, the African Plateau is continental, and the Columbia Plateau is volcanic or lava in origin.
The Pamir and parts of Bolivia, Peru and Colombia are identified with intermontane plateaus.
The Peninsular, Indian, Arabian and Australian plateaus are all classified as continental plateaus.
Parts of both Brazil and Siberia are identified as areas having volcanic or lava plateaus.
The Panna, Bhander, Rewa and Rohtas Plateaus are all identified as fluvial plateaus.
Domed plateaus are characterised by broad dome-like uplift, and the Ozark Plateau is an example of this type.
The Tibetan Plateau covers 2.5 million square kilometres; the Pamir is the “Roof of the World”; Meseta is in the Iberian Peninsula; and the Iberian Peninsula includes Spain.
The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient, relatively stable landmass.
V-shaped valleys occur in the upper or middle river course; rift valleys result from faulting or divergence; Death Valley is a rift valley; and blind valleys end abruptly.
A gorge is a deep, narrow and steep-sided river valley formed by river erosion.
A horst is an uplifted fault block, while a graben is a down-faulted block.
Vertical erosion forms gorges.
A canyon results from intense, prolonged erosion.
Deposition forms floodplains.
An estuary
is a drowned river mouth.
An estuary is a
funnel-shaped tidal mouth
Deltas occur along shallow coasts.
A canyon is a more deeply or widely eroded gorge.
Chisapani Gorge is a gorge.
Glacial erosion transforms a V-shaped valley into a U-shaped valley, while a less-erosive tributary glacier may leave a hanging valley with a waterfall at its junction.
A fjord is a deep, narrow sea inlet.
Drumlins are glacial depositional, streamlined oval hills, while eskers are formed by meltwater deposition.
An esker is a
long, winding ridge
Wind removal forms deflation hollows.
A uvala consists of coalesced dolines.
Wave-cut platforms form through cliff retreat.
The Indo-Gangetic Plain is an alluvial plain.
Horsts and grabens are associated with block mountains.
Waterfalls are sudden vertical falls, oxbow lakes are crescent-shaped, and estuaries are shaped by erosion or tidal flushing, strong tides and a generally single funnel-shaped opening.
An arête is a knife-edged ridge formed when two cirques erode a ridge, while a horn is a sharp pyramidal peak formed by several cirques eroding a mountain.
Evaporation or deposition forms playas.
The Northern Plains contain Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, and Khadar.
The Indian Desert includes the Thar, dunes and the Rann, while Konkan, Malabar, Northern Circars and Coromandel are Indian coastal plains.
The Andaman–Nicobar Islands have volcanic, coral, or tectonic origins.
The Chambal is associated with
ravines and badland topography
Western Ghats rivers are short and swift and generally have estuarine mouths.
The Rann of Kutch is described both as a salt marsh and as a seasonal marshy desert.
Barren Island is an active volcano, whereas Narcondam is volcanic and inactive-dormant.

constitutes approximately 78% of the atmosphere and is the most abundant gas.

of the atmosphere and is a major inert gas.

Strong solar heating and convection at the equator make the air rise higher, causing a higher tropopause and a thicker troposphere.
Temperature increases with altitude in the stratosphere.
Almost all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere.
Meteors are the most important association of the mesosphere.
Nitrogen is an essential nutrient, oxygen supports respiration and combustion, carbon dioxide supports photosynthesis and the greenhouse effect, and ozone absorbs harmful UV radiation.

Carbon dioxide is concentrated relatively low in the atmosphere, up to approximately 20 km.
The exosphere has extremely low density.
The early atmosphere had little or no free oxygen, whereas biological evolution altered the atmosphere to one dominated by nitrogen and oxygen.
Dust particles act as condensation nuclei.
Oxygen constitutes approximately 21%, carbon dioxide 0.04%, water vapour 0–4%, and ozone occurs in trace amounts.
The dry-air composition sequence is N₂ > O₂ > Ar > CO₂.
Permanent gases maintain relatively constant proportions, whereas variable gases change in amount across space and time.
Neon, helium, xenon, hydrogen and krypton
occur as trace minor gases in the atmosphere.
Water vapour contributes to humidity, clouds, precipitation and the greenhouse effect.
Methane and nitrous oxide
are identified as greenhouse gases.
The stratosphere is the second layer and extends approximately from 13 or 18 km to 50 km, with increasing temperature and ozone as its identity.
The troposphere is the lowest atmospheric layer.
Tropospheric temperature generally decreases with height, and the normal lapse rate is 6.5°C per kilometre, approximately 1°C per 165 metres.
Temperature is higher near the surface, lower at higher altitudes, and very low at the tropopause.
The tropopause separates the weather-dominated troposphere from the relatively stable stratosphere.
The stratosphere is suitable for jet aircraft.
The ozone layer is mainly in the stratosphere, consists of O₃ molecules containing three oxygen atoms, absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, and protects life from excessive ultraviolet exposure.
The mesosphere lies above the stratosphere, becomes colder upward, is the region where meteors burn or ablate, ends at the mesopause, and is very cold.
Radio communication is closely associated with the ionosphere.
High temperatures are the most important association of the thermosphere.
Solar charged particles interact with the upper atmosphere or magnetic environment.
The exosphere consists predominantly of very light gases and gradually merges with outer space.
The thermosphere begins at approximately 80 km and extends upward.
The traditional approximate region of the ionosphere is
The exosphere has an outer limit rather than a definite height.
The modern atmosphere is oxygen-rich and contains significant oxygen, whereas the early atmosphere contained CO₂, CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O among other gases.
Interaction between the biosphere and atmosphere provides the basis for biological evolution altering atmospheric composition.
